summary:
AgroField: Crop rotations powered by NASA data

Every field has its own story of heat, rain and soil. But most farmers still repeat the same rotation year after year, even as the climate changes.

AgroField helps farmers decide what to plant over the next two years, using data from their own field.

It works in any web browser, with no sign-up. First, you draw your field on a satellite map, or upload your survey plan as a KML, Shapefile or DXF file. Instantly, the app calculates the area, the terrain from NASA SRTM, and the water your soil can hold. If you already have a drone survey, you can upload it for higher precision.

Then you answer three quick questions: what you plant today, whether you can irrigate, and what matters most to you.

AgroField compares your current rotation with smarter alternatives, using fifteen years of daily climate data from NASA POWER. It shows the risk of heat during flowering, the water in the soil at sowing, and how much irrigation each crop would need.

Need more detail? Request a drone survey from our partner pilots at Vuelo Verde, straight from the app.

AgroField: satellite history, drone precision, better decisions.
details: What it does. AgroField is a free web app that helps farmers in the rainfed drylands of Santiago del Estero, Argentina, decide which two-year crop rotation to try before sowing, using NASA data for their own field rather than a regional average. It works in three steps: Your field: the farmer draws the field on satellite imagery or uploads the survey plan (KML, shapefile, GeoJSON or a DXF cadastral plan in the local POSGAR projection). The app immediately returns the area, the slope from NASA SRTM and the soil's plant-available water from ISRIC SoilGrids. Your season: the current rotation, irrigation (drip, sprinkler or canal, each with its own FAO efficiency) and the farmer's priorities. Your options: the current rotation side by side with the best-scoring alternative, with reasons, risks and a 24-month calendar. How it works. A transparent rule engine, not a black box, uses 15 years of NASA POWER daily climate (2011–2025) for that exact point. It computes Hargreaves reference evapotranspiration, crop water supply and deficit, frost risk, heat during flowering, and a daily two-layer soil-water balance. Each past season is classified as El Niño or La Niña with NOAA's ONI, so the farmer sees what actually happened on their field in each phase, which matters now with a very strong El Niño underway. ECOSTRESS (ECO_L3T_JET.002) adds measured actual evapotranspiration at 70 m. A 7-day forecast tells the farmer when to hold irrigation and which days are calm and dry enough to spray. Every number shows its source and whether it is observed, modelled or assumed. From satellite to field. The app plans drone work on the rotation's calendar: survey flights, an NDVI variable-rate prescription by vigour zones, cover-crop seeding and spraying. If the farmer owns a drone, the plan uses its specifications. If not, the request goes by WhatsApp or email to Vuelo Verde, a local drone-service company and our territorial partner. Our motto: satellites give the history, AgroField plans, drones confirm. Benefits and impact. Better decisions at the cheapest moment, before inputs are spent. Less wasted water and fewer chemicals, more months with living cover on the soil, and a printable sheet for the farmer's agronomist. Next, we want to run a pilot near Añatuya with a real field, comparing the plan with what the drone measures. Tools. TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet and Leaflet-Geoman, Turf, proj4, geotiff.js, shpjs, dxf-parser, zod and Vitest (over 180 automated tests). It is hosted on Vercel, with serverless functions for ECOSTRESS and the user backend (Supabase: magic-link sign-in, saved fields and history). It installs on a phone or tablet and opens offline, which matters in rural areas with little signal. The interface is in Spanish and English. What makes it creative. It starts from the farmer's real field boundary, not a pin on a map. It explains its reasoning instead of handing down a verdict. It turns El Niño into "what happened on your field in those seasons". And it links satellite data to concrete fieldwork through a local drone network. Factors we considered. Rainfed farming where rain decides everything, poor rural connectivity, farmers who are not data experts, and honesty about uncertainty: scores are guidance indices, not probabilities, and missing data is never invented. We also worked with the people who will use it, starting with an interview with Vuelo Verde.
